items.claim: Webb had to fold for launch because its operational configuration was too large for the available rocket.
items.synthesisExcerpt: Webb was designed to fold into the Ariane 5 fairing because its operational configuration was too large for the available rocket.
items.sourceEvidence: “Webb's fully deployed operational configuration is far too large to fit into any available rocket so it was designed to fold into a compact launch configuration that fit inside the Ariane 5.”
items.qualification: Keep this to launch context; do not broaden into Webb’s architecture.

items.claim: Deployment had many potential failure points, and a repair mission was not possible at Webb’s distance from Earth.
items.synthesisExcerpt: Deployment involved more than 50 major steps and over 300 possible single points of failure; the source says any one could have diminished or crippled the mission, and repair was not possible at Webb’s distance from Earth.
items.sourceEvidence: “There were over 50 major deployment steps, with 178 release mechanisms that had to perform perfectly or any one of over 300 single points of failure could have diminished or crippled the mission.” The source also says: “Since Webb operates at approximately 1 million miles from Earth, there was no possibility for a repair mission.”
items.qualification: These were potential risks; the source does not report that a deployment failure occurred.

items.claim: Webb reached its fully deployed operational configuration in its second week after launch.
items.synthesisExcerpt: By the second week, the secondary mirror and both primary-mirror wings had unfolded and latched, completing the telescope’s fully deployed operational configuration.
items.sourceEvidence: “During the second week after launch, we finished deploying the telescope structures by unfolding and latching the secondary mirror tripod and rotating and latching the two primary mirror wings. This brought Webb into its fully deployed operational configuration.”
items.usefulness: Marks the point when physical deployment was complete.
items.qualification: This was not the start of routine science operations.

items.claim: Cooling took several weeks, and mirror alignment continued during months two through four.
items.synthesisExcerpt: In the first month, the telescope and instruments cooled for several weeks. Mirror alignment took place in months two through four, followed by instrument-mode calibration in months five and six.
items.sourceEvidence: “The telescope and scientific instruments started to cool rapidly in the shade of the sunshield, but it took several weeks for them to cool all the way down and reach stable temperatures.” The source describes “the second, third and fourth months” as the period for “Initial optics checkouts, and telescope alignment.”
items.usefulness: Shows that reaching deployed configuration was followed by extended commissioning.
items.qualification: The source describes planned cooling and alignment, not recovery from a deployment failure.

items.claim: Instrument-mode calibration occupied months five and six; routine science operations began after six months.
items.synthesisExcerpt: Mirror alignment took place in months two through four, followed by instrument-mode calibration in months five and six. Webb began routine science operations after six months.
items.sourceEvidence: “In the fifth and sixth months: Calibration and completion of commissioning. We meticulously calibrated all of the scientific instruments’ many modes of operation while observing representative targets.” The source adds: “After six months: ‘Science operations!’ Webb began its science mission and started to conduct routine science operations.”
items.usefulness: Completes the timeline from deployment to routine use.
items.qualification: The source gives no detailed calibration results beyond the transition to routine science operations.

endpoint: Webb began routine science operations after six months of commissioning.
limitations: The source reports smooth deployment and does not identify specific anomalies or problems.
Do not portray commissioning as recovery from deployment failure.
Detailed calibration results are not provided.
